title: Milestone: The Living Ocean
objective: After this level you can connect the ocean's water, floor and life into one picture.
summary: The ocean averages about 3,700 m deep, but its food is made in roughly the top 5%. Sunlight feeds phytoplankton, kelp and reef algae, and they feed everything else, up to the sharks.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Let's put the living ocean in one picture.
cards.body: In Chapter 1 you learned how big, salty and dark the ocean is. In this chapter you met its life, from drifting plankton to sharks. Now join them up: where does all that life get its energy?

cards.headline: The kitchen is on the top floor
cards.body: From Chapter 1: the ocean averages about 3,700 m deep, and below about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis. So the ocean's food makers (phytoplankton, kelp and the algae inside reef corals) all work in roughly the top 5% of an average water column. The ocean is deep, but its kitchen is a thin sunlit skin on top.
cards.callout: About 200 m of light over about 3,700 m of water

cards.headline: Who eats sunlight, and who eats the eaters

items.label: Food makers
points: Phytoplankton, kelp and reef algae catch sunlight
Coral algae pass up to 90% of their food to the coral

items.label: Everyone else
points: Zooplankton, including jellyfish, mostly eat phytoplankton
Leatherbacks eat jellyfish; dolphins herd fish schools
Sharks at the top keep the whole web in balance

cards.headline: Milestone: the living ocean
learned: Why nearly all ocean life depends on a thin sunlit layer where plankton, kelp and reef algae make food.
How coral and the algae inside it trade shelter for food to build reefs packed with life.
Why fish swim in schools, and how thousands can turn as one with no leader.
How top predators like sharks and sea otters keep a whole ecosystem in balance.

questions.prompt: Living Ocean milestone, from Level 1: about how much of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean?

options.label: About a tenth
options.rationale: Far more than that.

options.label: About a quarter
options.rationale: Still too low.

options.label: About half
Nearly all of it
options.rationale: Land plants make much of the rest.

questions.explanation: About half of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean, mostly made by photosynthesizing plankton.

questions.prompt: Living Ocean milestone, from Level 41: what is Prochlorococcus?

options.label: The largest kelp species in the Pacific
options.rationale: That's giant kelp.

options.label: The smallest photosynthetic organism on Earth
The algae living inside reef corals
options.rationale: Those are a coral's lodgers; Prochlorococcus drifts free.

options.label: A jellyfish that leatherbacks eat
options.rationale: It's a tiny photosynthesizer, not a jellyfish.

questions.explanation: Prochlorococcus is the smallest photosynthetic organism on Earth, yet it makes up to 20% of the oxygen in our biosphere.

questions.prompt: Living Ocean milestone, from Level 43: why can so many species live on a coral reef?

options.label: Reef water is colder and richer in oxygen
options.rationale: Reefs grow in warm water.

options.label: Sharks never visit reefs, so it's safe
options.rationale: Sharks help keep reefs in balance.

options.label: Its structure offers food, shelter and nurseries
Reefs grow in the deep, where there's more room
options.rationale: Reef builders need shallow, sunlit water.

questions.explanation: Polyps build a structure full of hideouts where fish, crabs and turtles feed, shelter and raise young.

questions.prompt: Living Ocean milestone, from Level 47: a pinniped with small ear flaps is barking loudly on a dock. What is it?

options.label: A true seal
options.rationale: Seals have ear holes and are quiet.

options.label: A walrus
options.rationale: The clues point to a sea lion.

options.label: A young dolphin
options.rationale: Dolphins aren't pinnipeds.

options.label: A sea lion

questions.explanation: Ear flaps and a loud bark are sea lion clues; seals have only ear holes and grunt softly.

questions.prompt: Living Ocean milestone: photosynthesis stops at about 200 m, and the ocean averages about 3,700 m deep. Roughly what share of an average water column can make food from sunlight?

options.label: About 5%
About 25%
options.rationale: Too much: 200 m is a small slice of 3,700 m.

options.label: About 50%
options.rationale: Far too much.

options.label: About 95%
options.rationale: That's roughly the share left in the dark.

questions.explanation: 200 m out of about 3,700 m is about 5%: a thin sunlit skin over a deep, dark ocean.

questions.prompt: Living Ocean milestone: why do kelp forests and reef-building corals both stay in shallow water?

options.label: Both are animals that must breathe air
options.rationale: Kelp is an alga; corals live underwater.

options.label: Both depend on sunlight for photosynthesis
Both are anchored to beaches at low tide
options.rationale: They live underwater, not on beaches.

options.label: Both need the warm water of the tropics
options.rationale: Kelp likes cool water; light is the link.

questions.explanation: Kelp photosynthesizes, and reef corals rely on algae that do; both need light, which fades with depth.

questions.prompt: Living Ocean milestone: a leatherback crosses the Pacific on a diet of jellyfish. How does that meal trace back to phytoplankton?

options.label: Jellyfish are phytoplankton, so it eats sunlight directly
options.rationale: Jellyfish are animals: zooplankton.

options.label: It doesn't; jellyfish make their own food
options.rationale: Jellyfish are animals, not photosynthesizers.

options.label: Leatherbacks also graze on kelp forests
options.rationale: Their diet is soft open-ocean prey like jellyfish.

options.label: Jellyfish are zooplankton, which mostly eat phytoplankton

questions.explanation: Jellyfish are zooplankton; most zooplankton eat phytoplankton, the sunlight-powered foundation of the food web.
